newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FNB sees bad debts slowing in H2.
newsitem.headline: FNB sees bad debts slowing in H2.

text.p: First National Bank Holdings Ltd, one of South Africa's big four banking groups, said on Wednesday a large 64 percent surge in bad debts in the half year to end March was unwelcome, although it had been expected.

The bank, which on Wednesday reported six month results slightly below analysts' expectations, said the steady increase in bad debts -- which weighed at year end last year -- seemed to be tapering off.

"That 64 percent increase, while unwelcome, is not unexpected given where the consumer is in South Africa in the economic cycle with the high interest rates," Viv Bartlett, FNB managing director told Reuters.
"But we do believe, and we are hoping that they have plateaued out..," he said in an interview.
FNB earlier reported a 6.7 percent improvement in half year headline earnings to 110.4 cents a share, below a Reuters analysts' consensus poll of 112.0 cents.
The charge for bad and doubtful debts jumped 64.5 percent to 363.9 million rand from 221.2 at the halfway stage last year.
Amid tight credit conditions and following a commitment made at year end to shed underperforming units, FNB recently sold off two instalment credit units.

Asked if any other units faced the axe, Bartlett said: "That is all under review. We have not fingered anyone at this stage...The rest of the group is such that on a month-on-month basis they are profitable. There is not that degree of pressure."
FNB in December sold back a portion of its FirstPref division to McCarthy Retail Ltd and last month disposed of the debtor's book of Protea Furnishers Ltd.
Johan Meiring, an executive director of the bank, said that vehicle instalment bank Wesbank was experiencing a tough period.

"Wesbank is suffering...it is unwelcome but it is to be expected...The bad debts are high and they should be high at this moment in the economic cycle with the consumer under enormous stress," Meiring said.

He added, however, that Wesbank, being very sensitive to interest rate movements would benefit considerably if rates were cut -- a move FNB expects if credit inflation moves down in the next few months.
